attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated as a conclusion he draws from his chart.

semantics.note: A firm, unhedged claim about a trend that is getting worse. The normalised wording matches the statement.

contract.note: Reading 'worse' as a slower or smaller conversion of capex into capacity is the ordinary reading. Treating the D&A/capex ratio as a proxy rather than the outcome is fair. The baseline and the measure are unspecified, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own disclosure that dock-to-live times fell nearly 50% at one company. This is material counterevidence, but it covers only installation, not purchase-to-service, and does not settle the four-company trend the contract requires.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched-cohort commissioning data for the four hyperscalers. Microsoft's dock-to-live improvement runs against the claim, but it is a company disclosure about one firm and one stage. The contract says that cannot settle a group-level trend.

attribution.note: Zitron's own estimate in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps both 'I estimate' and 'maybe'. 'Maybe' is a possibility hedge on the figure, so the claim is not scored under policy.

contract.note: The contract scores hedged language on a plain reading, which policy does not allow. The annualisation, the compute-only scope and the treatment of internal compute were all supplied by the evaluator, not by the speaker.

evidence.note: Microsoft Cloud revenue is broader than AI compute, does not exclude the two labs, and is a single company's disclosure. It does not match the metric.

reviews.rationale: The figure is hedged with 'maybe' on top of 'I estimate', so it is a possibility, not a firm claim. The packet would not settle it anyway: there is no market-wide estimate of compute spending excluding the two labs.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps 'it appears' and the limit to his sources. 'Appears' marks a tentative, lower-confidence judgment, which policy treats as not scored.

contract.note: The contract itself calls the claim tentative, yet scores it on a plain reading, which policy forbids for hedged language. The two-year threshold, the definition of 'data center' and the August 2026 window were all chosen by the evaluator.

evidence.note: Epoch (Nov 2025): 1 to 3.6 years to reach 1 GW, partly from projected dates. Earlier than the target window.
JLL (Jan 2026): average build time of 18 months for a 50 MW facility. Not specific to large AI campuses.
NVIDIA 10-Q calls infrastructure development a multi-year process. This is broader than construction and gives no figures.

reviews.rationale: 'It appears', limited to the sources he can see, is a tentative judgment, so it is not scored. Even if it were, the evidence is mixed: 18 months for 50 MW, 1 to 3.6 years at GW scale. That would leave it unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own causal claim in his own post.

semantics.note: A firm causal claim: the backlogs come from the two labs' contracts, not from broad demand. The normalised wording matches.

contract.note: Reading the claim as 'the labs predominantly explain each provider's backlog' is fair and ordinary. Not crediting labs with contracts placed through intermediaries without evidence is reasonable.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own disclosure that all sequential RPO growth came from customers other than frontier model companies. This is growth, not the makeup of the backlog stock, which the contract says cannot settle composition.
Nebius's own disclosure of a Meta deal worth up to $27B: a large non-lab commitment. Nebius's total backlog makeup is not shown, so whether labs dominate is not settled.
Secondary report: Anthropic's deal roughly doubled Nscale's backlog to about $103B. This supports the claim for Nscale only, and it falls after the target quarter.

reviews.rationale: The evidence covers three of the seven providers, and only partly. Nscale leans toward the claim. Microsoft and Nebius point to substantial demand from others, but neither shows what the backlog stock is made of. There is no matched breakdown by ultimate customer, and no evidence that the backlogs overstate demand.
